title: Variables, Types and Expressions
oneLiner: int, double, decimal, bool, string and char in both languages, integer division and modulo, overflow, converting between types, and null versus None.
keyTakeaway: In C#, int divided by int is an int (7 / 2 is 3) and an int silently wraps past 2,147,483,647; Python's / always gives a float, // floors, and its ints never overflow. Binary floating point (double, float) can't store 0.1 exactly, so use decimal for money and never compare floats with ==.
explanation:
A variable is a name for a value, so you can store something and use it later. Every value has a type, the kind of value it is, and the type decides what you can do with it: you can divide numbers, but not text. C# makes you state the type when you create a variable (or lets the compiler work it out with var), and then the variable can only ever hold that type. Python attaches the type to the value instead, so the same name can point at a number now and text later.

Numbers come in two families. Integers are whole numbers (C#'s int and long, Python's int). Floating point numbers have a fractional part and are stored in binary (C#'s double and float, Python's float), which is fast but means values like 0.1 are stored as the nearest binary fraction, slightly off. For values that must be exact in base 10, such as money, both languages have a decimal type.

An expression is any piece of code that produces a value, such as 2 + 3 * 4 or price * quantity. The operators mostly match between the languages, with two differences that catch people constantly: what division does with two whole numbers, and how the remainder operator (%) treats negative numbers. Converting a value from one type to another (text to number, double to int) is where data from the outside world enters a program, so it's also where many errors start. Finally, null (C#) and None (Python) are how each language says "there's no value here", and using one as if it were a value is the most common crash in both.
